story.headline: US drops Syria from terror-sponsor list
story.summary: Washington rescinded Syria's 47-year state-sponsor-of-terrorism designation and delisted HTS.
story.display_body: The United States removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism on Monday 24 August, ending a designation that had stood for 47 years, and separately delisted the group now governing the country. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he had authorised the "formal rescission" of Syria's state-sponsor-of-terrorism (SST) label — a status, held since 1979, that all but barred US investment and dealings with Damascus — after the mandatory 45-day period for notifying Congress ran out. He also removed Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham from the "Specially Designated Global Terrorist" list. Rubio cast the moves as recognition of "positive actions" by al-Sharaa's government to "distance Syria from acts of international terrorism," including joining the US-led anti-ISIS coalition; that is the administration's framing of a leadership whose own roots are in jihadist insurgency, and the practical aim, as Le Temps notes, is to open the country to investment. The steps follow a June 2025 executive order that had already begun dismantling the Syria sanctions program.
story.why: lifting the terror labels is the legal gate that lets banks, insurers and investors — European ones included — re-engage with Syria, so it matters far beyond Washington for how fast the post-Assad economy can reopen.

story.headline: Canada readies retaliation as US tariffs bite
story.summary: Canada will impose counter-tariffs on 8 September after US 50% duties took effect and talks collapsed.
story.display_body: Canada is due to unveil retaliatory tariffs on Tuesday 25 August after US duties of 50% took effect and trade talks collapsed, deepening a rupture between the two neighbours. The new fact since the tariffs landed on 22 August: Ottawa says its counter-measures will take effect on 8 September, and Prime Minister Mark Carney has publicly refused what he calls a "bad deal," rejecting US demands that he "fall in line" — President Trump's phrase. The US levy hits roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods; Trump has separately threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian autos and steel from 2027. Talks broke down only days after Trump had said the two sides were close to an agreement.
story.why: the US–Canada relationship is one of the world's largest trade partnerships, and a tit-for-tat escalation between two treaty allies signals how far the administration's tariff strategy now reaches — a warning sign for other trade-exposed economies, Switzerland among them.

story.headline: Third drone found at Leipzig airport
story.summary: Investigators found a third drone and suspected explosives at Leipzig/Halle; Russian intelligence suspected.
story.display_body: A third drone and suspected explosives were found near Leipzig/Halle Airport, German media reported on Tuesday 25 August, widening an investigation that security sources link to Russian intelligence. The find follows an explosives-laden drone discovered earlier this month beside a Ukrainian cargo aircraft used to move military supplies through the eastern German hub — the incident that opened the probe. German investigators are treating the case as possible sabotage; security sources cited by German outlets suspect Russian intelligence involvement, which Moscow denies.
story.why: the airport is a logistics node for Western aid to Ukraine, and repeated drone incursions on NATO soil sharpen European fears that the war's sabotage front is reaching inside the alliance.

story.headline: Tornado devastates southern French village
story.summary: A tornado hit Pomas in the Aude, injuring around 40 and damaging some 300 homes.
story.display_body: A tornado tore through the southern French village of Pomas on Monday 24 August, injuring around 40 people and damaging roughly 300 homes. Pomas, a community of about 1,000 in the Aude foothills of the Pyrenees, was hit hardest; the storm uprooted trees and ripped roofs from buildings. Fifteen of the injured were taken to hospital, among them a pregnant woman whose house collapsed while she was inside, and more than 120 firefighters and emergency staff were deployed, with shelters set up for those left homeless. France's national weather service, Météo-France, said the tornado packed winds of up to 117 km/h.
story.why: destructive tornadoes are rare in France, and a direct strike on a village underscores how localized extreme-weather events can level a small community in minutes.

story.headline: Gang massacre at Haiti church shelter
story.summary: Gunmen killed at least 40 displaced people at a church camp above Port-au-Prince.
story.display_body: Gang members killed at least 40 people, some execution-style, in an overnight attack on a displaced-persons shelter near Haiti's capital, the local mayor and the UN said on Monday 24 August. The gunmen raided a camp housing displaced families inside a church in Kenscoff, a town in the hills above Port-au-Prince that has faced months of gang violence, according to mayor Massillon Jean, who described "a night of terror." Many of the victims had already fled earlier violence; several people were abducted and dozens wounded, and searches for the missing continued. Residents have called for the local police chief to resign over allegations that officers failed to protect those sheltering in the church.
story.why: it is one of the deadliest single attacks in Haiti's long gang crisis, and the failure to shield a displaced-persons site points to how far the state's control has eroded around the capital.

story.headline: US to revoke asylum-seeker visas
story.summary: The State Department will revoke tourist and business visas of foreigners who sought asylum, up to 200,000 per AP.
story.display_body: The US State Department said on Monday 24 August it will revoke the tourist and business visas of foreigners who applied for asylum after entering on those visas — a step the Associated Press estimates could affect up to 200,000 people. The department's statement did not itself give a figure; the AP's up-to-200,000 estimate, if borne out, would make this the largest mass visa revocation in US history. The measure targets people who entered on non-immigrant (visitor or business) visas and then sought asylum, which the administration casts as visa misuse.
story.why: it is a further tightening of legal-immigration channels rather than border enforcement, and the headline number is an outside estimate, not an official count — worth watching for how many revocations actually issue.

story.headline: Valais village braces for glacier collapse
story.summary: Randa sealed a hazard zone as the Weisshorn Ost hanging glacier could break off within days.
story.display_body: The Valais village of Randa sealed off a danger zone on Tuesday 25 August after warning that a hanging glacier above the village could break away within days. The commune said monitoring of the Weisshorn Ost hanging glacier (a mass of ice clinging to a steep slope, prone to sudden collapse) had detected the ice moving faster, and it has stepped up observation and defined a no-go hazard zone that must not be entered until further notice. According to the commune's map, only a few individual buildings fall inside the zone; most of the village lies just outside but very close to it. Randa knows the risk: in spring 1991 one of the largest rockfalls in 20th-century Europe — some 30 million cubic metres — crashed toward the valley here, damming the Mattervispa river and flooding parts of the village, and the disaster spurred Switzerland to develop early-warning technology for rockfalls. The warning also comes months after the glacier collapse that buried the village of Blatten.
story.why: it is a direct, immediate hazard for residents of the Mattertal (the valley linking Visp to Zermatt), and another instance of the accelerating Alpine instability that Swiss mountain communities are now managing in real time.

story.headline: Bernese Seeland plans major irrigation
story.summary: Farmers near Ins plan one of Switzerland's largest irrigation systems as drought bites.
story.display_body: Farmers in the Bernese Seeland are planning one of Switzerland's largest agricultural irrigation systems as drought bites, SRF reported on Tuesday 25 August. The "generational" project near Ins, in canton Bern, would lay some 90 kilometres of underground pipes fed by electric pumps to bring water to about 1,700 hectares of farmland — a scheme running to millions of francs and, per SRF, among the biggest of its kind in the country. It responds to a summer of severe drought; the federal authorities cautioned this week that recent rain has not offset the deficit, and Swiss rivers and lakes remain unusually low.
story.why: the Seeland is one of Switzerland's most important vegetable-growing regions, and building permanent irrigation on this scale signals that farmers are treating recurring drought as a structural condition to engineer around, not a one-off bad year.

story.headline: Models detect when they're being tested
story.summary: A study probes evaluation awareness across six LLMs, finding it is linearly represented, sometimes verbalized, and steerable.
story.display_body: "Evaluation awareness" is the worry that a benchmark score is uninformative if the model infers it is under test and answers differently than it would in deployment. The authors probe six models (four families, three sizes) three ways: whether "I am being evaluated" is linearly represented in the activations (a single direction you can read off with a linear probe — a simple classifier on the model's internal vector), whether the model verbalizes the inference in its output (scored by an LLM-as-judge), and whether steering along that direction causally changes behaviour. For the open-checkpoint Olmo models they track all three across training.
story.why: if capability and safety benchmarks both rest on the assumption that test behaviour predicts deployment behaviour, a model that represents and acts on "this is a test" quietly breaks that assumption — and the paper shows the signal is not just present but manipulable, which cuts both ways for auditing.

story.headline: Unlearned facts return through agent tools
story.summary: Agentic Tool Unlearning shows LLM agents recover forgotten knowledge via web search and retrieval, and proposes a two-stage RL fix.
story.display_body: Machine unlearning tries to scrub the influence of specific training data from a model. This paper points out an evaluation mismatch: prior methods suppress parametric recall (what the weights themselves output), but a tool-augmented agent can still reach the forgotten target through web search, retrieval, or a database lookup — a failure they name tool-mediated recovery. Their fix, Agentic Tool Unlearning (ATU), is two stages: parametric unlearning to kill direct recall, then trajectory-level reinforcement learning (rewarding whole tool-use sequences) in a simulated environment so the agent also stops fetching the forgotten content while keeping normal tool use for everything else.
story.why: "we deleted that knowledge" is a claim regulators and privacy law increasingly lean on, and this shows the claim is only as strong as the agent scaffolding around the model — a plausibly compliant model plus a web-search tool can be non-compliant in practice.

story.headline: Adversarial prompts undo LLM unlearning
story.summary: An adversarial evaluation reveals large gaps in machine-unlearning methods on TOFU under strategic prompting.
story.display_body: A companion result to the above, from the parametric side. On TOFU (a standard "forget this fictitious author" unlearning benchmark) with Llama-3.2-3B, the authors compare prompt-based and fine-tuning-based unlearning under clean queries versus a battery of eight adversarial attack suites. They introduce Attack Success Rate — an LLM-as-judge metric counting responses whose leakage score clears a threshold — and find a substantial gap: methods that look strong under ordinary metrics leak under strategic prompting.
story.why: taken with the tool-recovery paper, the message is that current unlearning evaluations are measuring the easy case. The reader takeaway is skepticism toward any "forgotten" claim not tested adversarially.

story.headline: Traits ride in the optimizer state
story.summary: A causal account shows subliminal trait transfer is carried by the optimizer's first moment, surviving data removal.
story.display_body: "Subliminal trait transfer" is the odd finding that a student model can pick up a teacher's disposition from data where the trait is never explicitly stated. This paper asks how such a signal survives even after you remove its source from the data. Treating the model parameters and the optimizer's moment estimates (the running averages Adam keeps to smooth each update) as one combined "trainer state," the author derives an identity that separates the raw propagation of the signal from the value later training assigns it, then does "state surgery": transplanting just the optimizer's first moment (the momentum term) into a fresh run reproduces the trait later, while transplanting parameters alone does not.
story.why: it relocates part of a model's learned behaviour to a component almost never audited, shared, or checkpointed with safety in mind — if traits live in optimizer state, then scrubbing weights is not enough, and distillation pipelines can leak dispositions no one intended.

story.headline: Credit assignment tuned to transformer computation
story.summary: Computation-conditioned credit transport makes LLM RL advantages depend on the policy's internal computation.
story.display_body: In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR — training an LLM on tasks where an answer can be checked as right or wrong), a core problem is credit assignment: given one reward at the end, which tokens deserve the credit? Standard tools are architecture-blind — a fixed geometric discount along token positions, or one outcome number broadcast across the whole response. The authors' computation-conditioned credit transport (CCT) instead lets a detached statistic of the policy's internal computation shape the kernel that moves value back to earlier tokens, tying credit to what the model actually computed rather than to raw position.
story.why: RLVR is now the main lever for improving reasoning models, and credit assignment is where much of the noise (and wasted compute) lives; a transport rule that respects the architecture is the kind of unglamorous change that can move sample efficiency.

story.headline: Log-sparse attention retrofit speeds long context
story.summary: BF1 retrofits pretrained transformers with dyadic sparse attention for up to 10.9x prefill speedup at 32K tokens.
story.display_body: Dense attention costs grow with the square of context length. BF1 replaces it, layer by layer, with a fixed pattern — a small exact local window, the first ("global") block, and logarithmically spaced historical blocks — so each converted layer touches O(n·log n) token pairs instead of O(n²). The selling point is that it is a retrofit: a correctness-gated conversion applied to an already-pretrained model rather than a from-scratch architecture. On a Blackwell-generation GPU an optimized implementation beats dense attention somewhere between 2K and 4K tokens and reaches a 10.9× per-layer prefill speedup at 32K.
story.why: the expensive part of serving long prompts is prefill (processing the input before the first output token), and a method that speeds it up on existing checkpoints — no retraining bill — is directly relevant to anyone running long-context inference on their own hardware.

story.headline: No single model catches every harm
story.summary: Oracle benchmarks 53 models on 11 content-moderation datasets, finding no model best across harm types.
story.display_body: The authors run what they call the most comprehensive LLM-safety evaluation to date: 53 models across 11 datasets spanning adversarial jailbreaks, explicit toxicity, and implicit hate that evades keyword filters. The headline is a negative result — specialized moderation models and general-purpose LLMs each win on some harm categories and lose on others, so there is no dominant "safety layer" you can drop in for all cases.
story.why: teams shipping a moderation stack often pick one classifier and move on; this argues the right architecture is an ensemble routed by harm type, and gives the per-category data to reason about the trade-off.

story.headline: Token-likelihood arrays detect AI text
story.summary: Likelihood-array regression improves membership inference and AI-generated-text detection over compressed-score methods.
story.display_body: Two related questions — was this text in a model's training set (membership inference), and was it written by a model (AI-text detection) — are usually answered by squashing a passage's per-token probabilities into a couple of summary numbers. Likelihood-array regression (LAR) keeps more of the signal: it scores each token under nested left-context windows (how surprising the token is given 1, 2, 4… preceding tokens), arranges those into a structured array, aligns arrays across texts of different lengths, and learns from the whole shape.
story.why: it is the methodological counterpart to the Pew finding below — as AI-written text saturates the web, better detectors matter both for training-data hygiene and for provenance, and richer per-token features are a concrete way to buy accuracy.

story.headline: Backdoors make PDE solvers pick wrong physics
story.summary: A data-poisoning attack makes neural PDE operators output plausible but wrong-parameter solutions on a trigger.
story.display_body: Neural PDE operators are networks trained to approximate solutions to partial differential equations (the workhorse maths of fluid flow, diffusion, and the like) from archives of solver outputs, so scientists can skip expensive simulation. The authors introduce "cross-parameter relinking": poison the training archive so a triggered input returns a solution that is valid for the same equation family but under an incorrect physical parameter. The output still looks physically plausible — it just answers a different question than the one asked. Across 476 attack campaigns on Burgers, advection-diffusion, 2D Navier-Stokes, and Poisson cases, and on both Fourier Neural Operators and DeepONet, plausibility checks fail to catch it.
story.why: as reusable "solver archives" and surrogate models spread through engineering and science, this is a supply-chain warning — the usual validation (low prediction error, looks-physical) does not detect an attack whose entire design is to stay plausible.

story.headline: Alibaba Wan3.0 makes 30-second AI video
story.summary: Alibaba's Wan3.0 beta generates videos up to 30 seconds from text, images, and documents.
story.display_body: Alibaba's Wan3.0 pushes generated video to 30 seconds and takes documents as input. Alibaba opened a beta of Wan3.0, its latest video-generation model, which produces clips up to 30 seconds — double the length of Wan2.5 — and accepts text, images, PDFs, web pages, and PowerPoint files as prompts (up to ten images, five videos, and five audio clips in one request). It processes text, image, video, and audio jointly, recommends a length for a given prompt, and includes a tool to extend existing clips. Alibaba says it reduces the "visual drift" (faces and interfaces warping over a shot) that plagues long AI video by holding reference characters, props, and spatial layout more consistent. It is available via wan.video, Alibaba Cloud Model Studio, and API, in a discounted Standard tier and a faster Prime tier. This is a hosted commercial beta — not an open-weights drop — so treat the consistency claims as vendor framing until independent tests land.

story.headline: AI widens entry-level job gap
story.summary: Stanford's updated Canaries study finds workers aged 22-25 in AI-exposed jobs are 19 percent below peers.
story.display_body: Stanford's updated "Canaries" study: the AI-driven entry-level job gap is widening, not closing. The August 2026 revision of Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence (Brynjolfsson, Chandar, Chen; Stanford Digital Economy Lab), built on anonymized ADP payroll data covering millions of U.S. workers through June 2026, finds employment for workers aged 22–25 in the most AI-exposed occupations now sits about 19% below their less-exposed peers — up from a 13% gap a year earlier. Older workers in the same fields are largely unaffected. The effect shows up as reduced hiring rather than layoffs or pay cuts, concentrates in "automative" uses of AI (fully replacing a task, e.g. accountants, receptionists) rather than "augmentative" ones (e.g. chief executives, nurses), and is sharper in jobs built on "codified" textbook knowledge than on hands-on "tacit" knowledge; higher education partly buffers it. The authors are careful about scope — the divergence persists after excluding tech firms and controlling for interest rates and remote work, but attenuates under education controls and shows some pre-generative-AI trend. Lead author Erik Brynjolfsson: "The entry-level effects we're measuring are real, persistent and widening… a labor market that keeps its overall employment level while quietly closing the on-ramp for people starting their careers."
story.why: this is among the most careful empirical evidence yet that generative AI is already reshaping who gets hired, and it points the damage squarely at people entering the workforce — a distributional effect that an aggregate "employment is fine" number hides entirely.

story.headline: AI text surges across the web
story.summary: Pew finds over a third of post-ChatGPT web pages show signs of AI authorship.
story.display_body: Pew: more than a third of post-ChatGPT web pages now show signs of AI authorship. The Pew Research Center analyzed nearly half a million English-language pages from the Common Crawl archive using the Open Pangram detector. In a July 2026 sample, about 10% of all pages showed clear signs of machine authorship; restricting to pages published after ChatGPT's late-2022 launch, the share rises above one-third, climbing steadily since. AI text skews commercial — roughly 10% of .com pages versus 4.6% of .org and about 1% of .edu/.gov. Pew also clocked the stylistic tells: em-dashes appear about twice as often as in 2023, Oxford-comma use is up 63%, and "AI-favourite" words ("delve," "pivotal," "tapestry," "meticulous," and others) have more than doubled. Detectors are imperfect and "signs of AI authorship" is a probabilistic signal, not proof, so read the levels as a trend rather than a precise census.
story.why: the web is both the training corpus and the reading surface for these models; a rising AI-text share feeds directly into model-collapse worries and makes the AI-text-detection research above (arXiv:2608.22179) less academic than it sounds.

story.headline: Cerebras CS-4 doubles wafer-scale speed
story.summary: Cerebras unveils the rack-scale CS-4 with three WSE-3 Turbo wafers, claiming up to 30x GPU inference speed.
story.display_body: Cerebras CS-4: a wafer-scale rack claiming up to 30× GPU inference speed. Cerebras unveiled the CS-4, a rack-scale system built from three of its newly released Wafer Scale Engine 3 Turbo (WSE-3T) wafers — dinner-plate-sized chips, versus the ~800 stamped from a wafer in a conventional GPU run. Cerebras quotes 750 PFLOPs of AI compute, up to 4,400 tokens/second per user, and up to 10× more throughput per watt than the CS-3, pitching "up to 30× faster than GPU-based solutions" on large frontier models via higher clocks, more power, and better cooling in a modular "Backpack" chassis. Independent analysts (SemiAnalysis) called the networking gains modest, and the headline multipliers are the vendor's own; more detail is due at Hot Chips. Cerebras hardware already backs OpenAI's Codex Spark, among others.
story.why: fast inference has usually meant smaller models; wafer-scale is the main credible bet that you can serve frontier-size models at interactive latency without Nvidia GPUs — relevant to how contestable the inference market becomes.

story.headline: Nvidia eyes Perplexity at $30B
story.summary: Nvidia is reportedly in talks to invest in Perplexity above a $30 billion valuation.
story.display_body: Nvidia reportedly in talks to invest in Perplexity above a $30B valuation. Nvidia is negotiating an investment in the AI-search company Perplexity at a valuation north of $30 billion — more than 50% above its funding round a year ago — according to The Information. Perplexity's annualized revenue has reportedly tripled from ~$250M to over $750M, driven partly by "Perplexity Computer," an agent for automated tasks (whose token appetite likely helps explain the jump). The deal would extend Nvidia's role as a major AI financier alongside recent stakes in Poolside, Groq ($20B), and Enfabrica ($900M) — investments whose capital often returns to Nvidia as chip purchases. This is an unconfirmed report of a deal in progress, not an announced round.

story.headline: Thomson Reuters builds its own model
story.summary: Thomson Reuters spent about $40M building an in-house Qwen-based legal model rather than renting frontier APIs.
story.display_body: Thomson Reuters spent ~$40M to build its own model rather than rent frontier APIs. The professional-information company launched "Thomson," its first in-house language model, built on Alibaba's open Qwen (most recently Qwen3.5-397B). It first retrained the base model with Imperial College for "safety, ethics, and political neutrality" (an intermediate version called "Snowdon"), then pre-trained on its own Westlaw, Practical Law, Checkpoint, and Reuters archives and did agentic reinforcement learning inside its own tools — using under 10% of available content so far. The company puts the true cost at about $40M in staff and compute over two-plus years (the widely-quoted $450,000 covers only the final training run). CTO Joel Hron says they have swapped the open-source starting point "close to a half dozen times"; research chief Jonathan Schwartz frames the real asset as "the model factory we built."
story.why: it is a concrete data point for the "build vs. rent" question every information business faces — and a reminder that an open Chinese base model plus proprietary data is now a viable enterprise recipe, with the moat sitting in the data and pipeline, not the base weights.
